translationRepairs: After Xi was executed, his elder brothers Yi, Shu, and five others fled south one after another, so Tan inherited the title; his fief was changed to prince of Fucheng.
After Xi was executed, five elder brothers including Yi and Shu fled south one after another, so Tan inherited the title; his fief was changed to prince of Fucheng.
兄翼、樹等五人 marks a total of five elder brothers (Yi and Shu among them); “Yi, Shu, and five others” wrongly adds five more people, and the proposed wording restores the inclusive count.
After Xi was executed, his elder brothers Yi, Shu, and five others fled south in succession, so Tan was able to inherit; his fief was changed to Prince of Fucheng.
After Xi was executed, five elder brothers including Yi and Shu fled south in succession, so Tan was able to inherit; his fief was changed to Prince of Fucheng.
The same 等五人 construction on the literal field means five in all, not five beyond Yi and Shu; the replacement correctly states five elder brothers including Yi and Shu.
Yuan Bin, styled Shanjii — his grandfather was Emperor Xianwen of Wei.
Yuan Bin, styled Shanji — his grandfather was Emperor Xianwen of Wei.
字善集 romanizes as Shanji; Shanjii is a clear typographical doubling of the final i, and the proposed courtesy-name form matches the Chinese.
Yuan Bin, styled Shanjii, his grandfather was Emperor Xianwen of Wei.
Yuan Bin, styled Shanji, his grandfather was Emperor Xianwen of Wei.
The literal field has the same Shanjii typo for 善集; correcting to Shanji fixes the romanization without other semantic change.
His elder brother Prince Huaihuai Yu had no son; Xiaoyou was made to inherit the title.
His elder brother Prince Linhuai Yu had no son; Xiaoyou was made to inherit the title.
臨淮王 is Prince Linhuai; Huaihuai reverses/corrupts the place-name syllables, and Prince Linhuai Yu correctly renders 臨淮王彧.
His elder brother Prince Huaihuai Yu had no son; he had Xiaoyou inherit the title.
His elder brother Prince Linhuai Yu had no son; he had Xiaoyou inherit the title.
The literal sentence repeats Huaihuai for 臨淮; replacing it with Linhuai restores the correct title reading.
Gao Cheng said, "Prince Huaihuai has received the decree and is pardoned of guilt."
Gao Cheng said, "Prince Linhuai has received the decree and is pardoned of guilt."
Gao Cheng’s speech addresses 臨淮王; Prince Linhuai is the accurate title, whereas Huaihuai is the same corrupted romanization as in s0032.
Gao Cheng said: "Prince Huaihuai received the decree and is pardoned of guilt."
Gao Cheng said: "Prince Linhuai received the decree and is pardoned of guilt."
The literal quotation likewise requires Prince Linhuai for 臨淮王; the proposed fix matches the Chinese title.
Xiaoyou held office in Yin for many years, kept to the law, and won great repute; yet he lacked backbone, was adept at courting the powerful, and upright men scorned him for it.
Xiaoyou served as mayor (yin) for many years, kept to the law, and won great repute; yet he lacked backbone, was adept at courting the powerful, and upright men scorned him for it.
在尹積年 means years spent in the office of yin (mayor), not residence in a place named Yin; “served as mayor (yin)” correctly treats 尹 as the office title.
Xiaoyou accumulated years as mayor of Yin, held to the law himself, and won great repute; yet by nature he lacked backbone, was skilled at serving the powerful, and was mocked by the upright.
Xiaoyou accumulated years as yin (mayor), held to the law himself, and won great repute; yet by nature he lacked backbone, was skilled at serving the powerful, and was mocked by the upright.
The literal “mayor of Yin” likewise turns 尹 into a toponym; “yin (mayor)” restores the office-title reading without inventing a place.
